title: Chapter 155: More Than One Person
html:
Cooked meat hardened after prolonged exposure to air. Keeping his chest camera trained on the duck, Chen Ge touched it. The flesh remained soft and faintly warm.

“This was cooked less than an hour ago.” He shifted position and pulled the carcass from the cage. “The organs weren’t properly removed, someone snapped its neck by force, and the head is missing.”

He examined it closely. Teeth marks scarred the half-cooked flesh, and something had ripped open the belly. No feathers lay nearby, which meant whatever tore into the duck had swallowed feathers and meat together.

“Were these cages meant for large dogs?” After replacing the duck, he noticed two plastic bowls outside the bars, each filled with a clear liquid.

“Why two bowls? Did they keep two dogs in here?” The containers looked identical. He raised each to his nose. One was odorless and likely held ordinary water; the other gave off a faint, acrid smell.

“Rat poison.” Chen Ge recognized the scent because he had once bought poison to keep rats from chewing the Haunted House props.

“Two identical bowls—one water, one poison. Wasn’t the owner afraid an animal would drink from the wrong one?” The arrangement made no sense. He recorded everything, then glanced at his phone. Messages raced through the chat, and one fragment caught his eye: it mentioned a cage and a page.

He had no time to comb through the torrent of comments. Inspecting the bars, he found the cage door smeared with paint, as though someone with stained hands had clung to it and refused to let go.

“What if these cages weren’t meant for animals?” Empty medicine bottles littered the abandoned nurses’ station alongside small bags labeled with patients’ names. Some still contained strange pills. “Someone is living in a hospital abandoned for five years—and there appears to be more than one of them.”

Chen Ge grew more cautious. Every tool he had packed was meant for ghosts, not dangerous human squatters. As he left the nurses’ station, he studied both walls.

If someone had been dragged from the cage by force, paint on their hands would have left a trail during the struggle. A few steps away, gouges raked the wall, and blood streaked the peeling paint.

“They were injured?” He followed the marks upstairs. On the second floor, the corridor divided: one branch continued through the first sick hall, while the other connected to the second, confirming the map’s layout.

It took him twenty minutes to inspect the first building. He found no concealed spaces large enough to hide a person, no trace of the cage’s prisoner, and no further evidence of occupation.

“Were they dragged into another sick hall?” His phone vibrated as he descended the stairs. Liu Dao was calling.

“Yes?” Chen Ge was wound so tight that even this minor interruption jolted him.

“Chen Ge, you’re moving too fast! We planned an all-night broadcast, and you explored the entire first sick hall in twenty minutes. What will you do with the rest of the night?” Liu Dao had been monitoring the stream. “Qin Guang has passed six hundred thousand viewers, while you’ve barely reached fifty thousand. Don’t focus solely on exploring—interact with your audience.”

Listening, Chen Ge wandered back to the first floor. One glance down the corridor made his pupils contract. “Wait. Who closed the entrance? I left it open.”

“What did you say?” Liu Dao paused. “In any case, don’t feel too much pressure. Be careful.”

“All right. I’ll call you later.” He pocketed the phone and sprinted toward the entrance, mallet raised. Passing the nurses’ station, he glanced inside by habit. “Something changed.”

The front door took priority, so he did not stop to investigate. He grabbed the handle and shook it violently. “Damn it! It’s locked. When did that happen?”

Through the gap, he saw a new padlock hanging outside. He threw his shoulder against the door, but it did not budge.

“Whoever changed that lock did it quickly. This isn’t their first time.”

People were living in the abandoned hospital—most likely former patients who had returned. They were not unintelligent; from a certain perspective, they might be cleverer and more dangerous than ordinary people. Underestimating them could prove fatal.

His mallet failed to pry open the door. In the neighboring rooms, iron mesh sealed every first-floor window. Only then did he understand how the hospital’s patients must have felt: the entire building was a prison.

Ask for help? Call the police?His viewership was still rising. Leaving now would end the broadcast, and the Trial Mission required him to survive inside the Third Sick Hall until dawn. Police intervention would guarantee failure.

“The second-floor windows had no mesh. I can escape through one if necessary. For now, there’s no need to call the police.” Determined to complete the Trial Mission and uncover his parents’ clues, Chen Ge pressed on.

Back at the nurses’ station, he recognized the change: someone had overturned both plastic bowls, spilling their contents across the floor.

“Were they afraid I’d discover one contained poison?” He could not understand the act. As he started to rise, rows of tiny writing beneath the wooden counter caught his eye. He twisted around and leaned into the cramped space for a closer look. Before he drew near enough to read, something brushed the crown of his head—like worms burrowing into his hair.

He reached up. Something stroked the back of his hand. When he turned his head, his heart lurched.

Thick clumps of human hair had been taped beneath the counter.

Some strands were long, others short, and there was no telling where they had come from. “Why keep hair here? Did it belong to whoever was locked in the cage?”

A shrill feline snarl suddenly sounded outside the station. Chen Ge crawled out at once. The white cat bared its teeth at the stairs to the second floor, its mismatched eyes fixed on one particular spot.
